stem: What are the only two possible values of a `boolean` expression?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

explanation: Java's `boolean` type has exactly two possible values: `true` and `false`.

stem: In Java, what determines which statements are considered part of an `if` block when no curly braces `{}` are used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All statements indented at the same level as the if, regardless of braces
choices.explanation: Indentation is just a formatting convention in Java -- it has no effect on which statements belong to the if.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only the single statement immediately following the if condition
choices.explanation: Without braces, only the very next single statement is controlled by the if; anything after that runs unconditionally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All statements until the next blank line in the source file
choices.explanation: Blank lines have no syntactic meaning in Java.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All statements until the end of the method, ignoring indentation
choices.explanation: This would make the rest of the method conditional, which is not how Java's if statement works without braces.

explanation: Without braces, only the single statement immediately after the `if` condition is conditional; this is a common source of bugs.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: println("B") is NOT part of the if block (indentation doesn't matter in Java), so it always executes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The if condition is false, so println("A") does not execute at all.

explanation: Indentation is misleading here: without braces, only `println("A")` belongs to the `if`. Since the condition is false, only `println("B")` -- which is unconditional -- runs.

stem: What does `&&` represent in a boolean expression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Logical OR -- true if either operand is true, or both
choices.explanation: This describes ||, the OR operator, not &&.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Logical AND -- true only if both operands are true
choices.explanation: && (AND) requires both sides to be true for the whole expression to be true.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Logical NOT -- inverts a boolean value from true to false
choices.explanation: This describes !, the NOT operator, not &&.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: && is a logical operator for booleans, not an arithmetic or bitwise addition operator.

explanation: `&&` is the logical AND operator: the combined expression is true only when both operands are true.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: x (5) > 0 is true, and x (5) < 10 is also true, so true && true is true.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Both individual conditions are true, so the AND of them is also true, not false.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is a boolean expression, so it evaluates to true or false, not a number.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is a valid, properly parenthesized compound boolean expression.

explanation: Both `x > 0` and `x < 10` are true for `x = 5`, so the `&&` expression evaluates to `true`.

stem: Why is short-circuit evaluation of `&&` and `||` useful when the left operand is `x != 0` and the right operand involves dividing by `x`?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It makes the division happen faster by running the check in parallel
choices.explanation: Short-circuiting is about whether an operand is evaluated at all, not about making evaluated code run faster.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If x != 0 is false, Java skips the division, avoiding a divide-by-zero error
choices.explanation: With &&, if the left operand is false, the right operand is never evaluated -- so checking x != 0 first safely guards the division.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It guarantees the division will always be evaluated first, before the check
choices.explanation: This is backwards -- with &&, the left operand is evaluated first, and the right side may be skipped entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has no effect on whether the division is evaluated at all
choices.explanation: Short-circuiting directly determines whether the right-hand operand gets evaluated at all.

explanation: With `&&`, if the left operand is false, Java skips the right operand entirely -- so `x != 0 && 10 / x > 1` safely avoids division by zero.

stem: Which is the recommended way to compare the content of two String objects, regardless of how they were created?

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: .equals() always compares actual character content, regardless of how the String objects were created.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: length() only tells you how many characters a String has, not whether two Strings have the same content.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: + concatenates Strings; it doesn't compare them.

explanation: `.equals()` reliably compares String content and should be used instead of `==` for this purpose.
